The Committee’s cut to 1.50–1.75% and its “ample reserves” operating stance are consistent with the literature on how monetary policy supports real activity when inflation expectations are subdued and investment is soft. New Keynesian work (Galí and Gertler, 1999; Woodford, 2003; Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans, 2005) emphasizes expectations: with market-based inflation compensation low and core inflation below 2%, easing helps steer expected inflation toward target while stabilizing the output gap. On the real side, the investment function links capex to interest rates and internal finance; evidence on the bank-lending/internal-funds channel (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994) suggests lower rates and reliable funding via reserves and repo can mitigate financing constraints, supporting inventory and fixed investment. Empirical work (Romer and Romer; Sims and Zha) documents that such policy shocks transmit to output through the interest-rate channel, though heightened uncertainty can blunt investment responsiveness. Netting these, the tone is slightly positive—policy is supportive of continued expansion and re-anchoring inflation—but tempered by weak business investment/exports and muted inflation pressures.
